what_it_does: In a processor that executes instructions strictly one at a time in order (an in-order processor), a slow instruction — such as one waiting for data from main memory — blocks every later instruction, even those that do not depend on it. This paper explores adding value prediction to an in-order processor: the idea is that some instructions produce the same result repeatedly or in a predictable pattern, so the hardware can guess the result early, let later instructions proceed using that guess, and then correct any mistakes when the real result arrives. Because instructions execute in order, mistakes are cheap to fix — no complex rollback is needed, the real value just overwrites the guess in place. The paper integrates two forms of prediction — one that guesses load values based on the memory address (address-based), and one that extrapolates from past outputs of the same instruction — into a RISC-V (an open, freely licensed processor instruction set) core and redesigns the first-level cache to support speculative writes from predicted values.
